title: Scope and mobile threat models
concept: Separate device, application and backend security. Record the owned emulator, app build, test accounts and authorized API environment.
deeper: Map assets, entry points and trust boundaries. Owning a phone does not automatically authorize tests of every service it contacts.
practice: Draw the data flow for a fictional notes app: user, local storage, another app and test API.
question: What makes a test reproducible?
answer: A recorded build, OS/API level, starting state, inputs and expected result.

title: Android architecture and sandboxing
concept: Android combines a Linux kernel, native libraries, runtime, framework services and apps. App identities normally separate private files and processes.
deeper: Binder IPC, permissions and SELinux mediate crossings. Rooted or modified images change the assumptions of an assessment.
practice: Label the boundaries between a notes app, its database, a sharing activity and a backend.
question: Does an app permission grant root?
answer: No. It authorizes specific operations under platform rules.

title: Android Studio emulator lab
concept: Use a virtual device and a locally built training app with synthetic data. Record the image, API level, target SDK and app version.
deeper: Snapshots make exercises repeatable. Hardware-backed keys, biometrics and vendor behavior may differ on a physical phone.
practice: Create a baseline snapshot, install your own demo app and restore the snapshot after testing. No APK is supplied by this workbook.
question: Does an emulator result apply to every device?
answer: No. Confirm behavior on supported OS versions and hardware.

title: ADB and debugging trust
concept: ADB connects SDK tools to a device or emulator authorized for debugging. Explicit target selection avoids inspecting the wrong device.
deeper: USB authorization and wireless pairing establish trust. Revoke unused debugging trust after testing; available commands depend on the device build.
practice: Follow the workbook to list targets, read the emulator API level and inspect only your training package.
question: What does unauthorized in the device list mean?
answer: The device has not granted this workstation debugging trust. Approve only on your own unlocked test device.

title: APK structure and signing
concept: An APK includes a manifest, resources, DEX code and sometimes native libraries. Signing supports app identity and update integrity.
deeper: Split APKs may spread code and resources across packages. Reconstructed code is an approximation of source and may omit important context.
practice: Use APK Analyzer or JADX on your own build. Record package name, version, certificate digest and native libraries.
question: Does a valid signature prove safety?
answer: No. It establishes a signing relationship rather than harmless behavior.

title: Manifest and permissions
concept: Compare declared permissions and exported components with the features users expect. Review the merged release manifest.
deeper: Debuggable state, permission protection levels and component defaults affect exposure. Rules depend on platform version and target SDK.
practice: Compare debug and release manifests; deny an optional permission and verify graceful behavior.
question: Is every requested permission a vulnerability?
answer: No. Assess necessity, runtime behavior, consent and impact.

title: Storage, logs and backups
concept: Private files, databases, shared storage, logs and backups have distinct exposure paths. Minimize retained sensitive data.
deeper: A sandbox does not settle backup or compromised-device risks. Check account switching, logout cleanup and the difference between local deletion and server revocation.
practice: Store a fake token in your debug app. Inspect permitted app files and filtered logs, then verify the documented cleanup policy.
question: Does Base64 protect a token?
answer: No. It is reversible encoding, not encryption or access control.

title: Cryptography and Android Keystore
concept: Use established cryptographic APIs and managed keys. Android Keystore can restrict key use; hardware backing depends on the device and configuration.
deeper: Review key purpose, authenticated encryption, nonce handling, rotation and invalidation. Test failure handling when a key becomes unavailable.
practice: Trace one encrypted demo field from generation to decryption and document key storage and plaintext lifetime.
question: Does Keystore prevent every misuse of decrypted data?
answer: No. Application logic still controls plaintext and authorized operations.

title: Exported components and IPC
concept: Activities, services, receivers and providers can expose operations to other apps. Each reachable operation needs suitable validation and authorization.
deeper: Check caller identity, component selection, URI grants and query scope. Intent extras are inputs, not proof of trust. Review PendingIntent mutability.
practice: Create a table of component, caller, permission, input and expected rejection. Exercise malformed inputs in your app test suite.
question: Is exported=true always a defect?
answer: No. Some components intentionally serve others; access checks and data handling determine risk.

title: Deep links and verified App Links
concept: Deep links route URIs to app screens. Verified App Links associate supported web links with an app through domain verification.
deeper: Routing is separate from resource authorization. Parse links carefully and validate unexpected fields, redirects and signed-out behavior.
practice: Test a synthetic note link with an unknown identifier, missing session and unexpected query fields.
question: Can a verified link replace authorization?
answer: No. It does not grant access to the record named by the link.

title: WebView trust boundaries
concept: WebView embeds web content inside an app. JavaScript bridges can connect web input to native capabilities.
deeper: Restrict origins, navigation and bridge methods. Review local-file access and mixed content; check redirects as well as the initial URL.
practice: Draw allowed origins and bridge methods for a demo WebView. Verify that harmless unexpected navigation is rejected.
question: Is validating only the first URL sufficient?
answer: No. Later navigation can cross the intended boundary.

title: TLS and proxy traffic inspection
concept: Use Burp Suite or mitmproxy with a deliberately configured debug app to inspect synthetic requests and responses.
deeper: Certificate trust and pinning affect interception. A failed interception does not prove secure business logic. Keep debug CA trust out of release configuration.
practice: Compare captured fields with the data-flow diagram. Remove the temporary proxy and test CA settings after the exercise.
question: Should release certificate validation be disabled for testing?
answer: No. Use scoped debug settings and verify release validation separately.

title: Authentication and backend authorization
concept: The app is a client. The backend must enforce ownership and privileged actions independently of interface controls.
deeper: Review token expiry, refresh rotation, logout revocation and account switching. Local biometric prompts do not replace server-side checks.
practice: Using two synthetic accounts on your owned staging API, confirm that account B cannot read account A notes.
question: Is hiding an administrator button an access control?
answer: It is a UI choice; the server must reject unauthorized operations.

title: Static analysis tools
concept: JADX helps inspect reconstructed code, Apktool decodes resources and bytecode representation, and MobSF organizes automated review results.
deeper: Obfuscation, native code and dynamic loading limit visibility. A scanner warning needs a reachable code path and demonstrated impact.
practice: Review your training APK locally and validate one warning with code context, prerequisites, evidence and a proposed fix.
question: Does a clean scan prove security?
answer: No. Automated coverage is incomplete, especially for business logic.

title: Runtime observation and instrumentation
concept: Android Studio debugger, profiler and Logcat reveal behavior for chosen inputs. Frida supports instrumentation of an authorized training process.
deeper: Instrumentation can change timing, integrity signals and behavior. Capture an unmodified baseline before drawing conclusions from instrumented observations.
practice: Place a breakpoint before saving a dummy note in your debug app. Observe validation and file selection, then compare with static analysis.
question: Does one runtime path cover all behavior?
answer: No. State, input and environment select different paths.

title: Device hardening and incident indicators
concept: Review patch state, screen lock, installation sources, debugging trust and powerful access such as accessibility or device administration.
deeper: Boot integrity, SELinux and supported updates contribute to device security. Unlocking or rooting changes assumptions and may erase data; neither is required here.
practice: On a spare owned device, inventory settings through the UI. Correlate unfamiliar access grants with installation history before drawing conclusions.
question: Does battery drain alone prove spyware?
answer: No. Correlate observations and preserve evidence before changes during an investigation.

title: Privacy and SDK supply chains
concept: Dependencies can add permissions, endpoints and data collection. Track SDK purpose, version, recipients and retention.
deeper: Compare declared privacy expectations with synthetic test traffic. Protect signing keys and keep debug assets out of release artifacts.
practice: Create an SDK inventory and compare it with the merged manifest and observed data categories.
question: Does TLS make all collection appropriate?
answer: No. Collection still needs a purpose, appropriate consent and retention controls.

title: Assessment, reporting and regression
concept: Combine manifest, storage, IPC, network and backend checks into an evidence-based assessment. Prioritize practical impact and prerequisites.
deeper: Use applicable OWASP MASVS categories and current MASTG techniques. Record uncovered scenarios, tool limits and differences across OS versions.
practice: Reproduce one issue in an owned demo app, fix it, retest the failure case and a valid-use case, then restore the emulator.
question: What supports a remediation claim?
answer: Recorded results on the corrected build with negative and valid-use tests and explicit coverage limits.

title: Build an attack-surface map
concept: Map each external entry point to the sensitive action it can reach: exported components, deep links, shared files, WebViews, IPC and API calls.
deeper: Treat caller-controlled data as untrusted until validation and authorization occur. A manifest declaration alone does not establish a reachable exploit.
practice: Use APK Analyzer, JADX and the merged manifest to inventory entry points in your own app. Trace one input to a file read or backend request.
workflow: Record entry point, caller requirements, source of input, validation, privileged action and data returned. Compare signed-out and signed-in states with synthetic accounts.
evidence: A useful finding shows a boundary crossed and a reproducible effect. A component list is only an inventory.
remediation: Remove unused entry points; require appropriate caller permissions and validate at the action boundary. Retest both rejected and legitimate callers.
question: What evidence would distinguish a confirmed issue from a tool observation in this lesson?
answer: A useful finding shows a boundary crossed and a reproducible effect. A component list is only an inventory.

title: Intent redirection and delegated actions
concept: An app may accept an Intent inside another message and forward it. Forwarding untrusted destinations can turn the app into a deputy for a caller.
deeper: PendingIntent represents a delegated operation under its creator identity. Mutability, explicit destination and granted capabilities affect what the recipient can influence; creator identity does not authenticate every later sender.
practice: Review getParcelableExtra, startActivity and PendingIntent creation in owned source using JADX or Android Studio.
workflow: In a two-app emulator lab, have a test sender request a harmless screen. Compare an approved destination with an unexpected destination and record whether validation occurs before forwarding.
evidence: Capture caller, resolved component and allowed operation. A normal navigation event is not proof of arbitrary privilege.
remediation: Use explicit destinations and a narrow allowlist; avoid forwarding arbitrary nested Intents. Prefer immutable PendingIntents when mutation is unnecessary and grant only required capabilities.
question: What evidence would distinguish a confirmed issue from a tool observation in this lesson?
answer: Capture caller, resolved component and allowed operation. A normal navigation event is not proof of arbitrary privilege.

title: Content providers and file boundary testing
concept: Providers expose structured data or files through URIs. Authorization must constrain both the caller and the particular object accessed.
deeper: Path normalization, URI grants, SQL parameter handling and projection selection are separate controls. String-prefix checks alone can confuse sibling paths and canonical locations.
practice: Review provider query/openFile implementations and FileProvider paths in an owned demo app.
workflow: Create synthetic public and private records. Test a permitted URI, an unknown identifier, an unexpected projection and a path outside the intended fixture directory through the app test harness.
evidence: Record returned columns, rows, file identity and denial behavior. No result may mean a wrong test setup rather than correct enforcement.
remediation: Use narrowly scoped provider paths and temporary grants; parameterize queries and verify resolved paths remain within the intended root. Retest valid sharing after the fix.
question: What evidence would distinguish a confirmed issue from a tool observation in this lesson?
answer: Record returned columns, rows, file identity and denial behavior. No result may mean a wrong test setup rather than correct enforcement.

title: OAuth, PKCE and session lifecycle
concept: Mobile OAuth flows cross app, browser and authorization-server boundaries. Public clients cannot keep an embedded shared secret confidential.
deeper: PKCE binds authorization-code redemption to a verifier. State protects request correlation, while OIDC nonce serves a different purpose. Correct redirect handling and server validation remain necessary.
practice: Draw the authorization and callback flow for your staging identity provider. Use a browser and test accounts; redact all codes and tokens.
workflow: Check an ordinary login, cancelled login, unmatched state, expired code and logout. Verify account switching does not reuse another account session.
evidence: A rejected callback and a server trace support different claims. Never infer server revocation solely from clearing the app screen.
remediation: Use a maintained OAuth library and external user-agent flow, validate correlation, constrain redirects and enforce token lifetimes server-side. Retest recovery and normal sign-in.
question: What evidence would distinguish a confirmed issue from a tool observation in this lesson?
answer: A rejected callback and a server trace support different claims. Never infer server revocation solely from clearing the app screen.

title: WebView bridges and navigation chains
concept: Web content becomes dangerous when an untrusted origin reaches privileged native bridge methods or local app files.
deeper: The initial URL, redirects, subframes and later navigations can have different origins. URL substring matching is not an origin parser; scheme, host and port require explicit interpretation.
practice: Inspect addJavascriptInterface, navigation handlers and file-access settings in the owned app.
workflow: Use harmless pages in a controlled lab to compare approved and rejected origins, a redirect and a missing session. Observe whether a bridge method can be called without its expected prerequisites.
evidence: Record origin, navigation chain, exposed method and observed effect. JavaScript execution by itself is expected in many WebViews.
remediation: Remove unnecessary bridges, minimize callable methods and validate navigation with parsed origins. Apply native authorization to every sensitive bridge operation.
question: What evidence would distinguish a confirmed issue from a tool observation in this lesson?
answer: Record origin, navigation chain, exposed method and observed effect. JavaScript execution by itself is expected in many WebViews.

title: TLS trust, pinning and release validation
concept: TLS validates the endpoint and protects transport. Debug trust, certificate pinning and backend authorization solve different problems.
deeper: User CA behavior depends on target SDK and configuration. A pinning failure can block observation while the API still contains logic flaws. Rotation must preserve security and availability.
practice: Compare release and debug Network Security Configuration with Android Studio; inspect synthetic traffic through Burp or mitmproxy in the approved debug build.
workflow: Test a valid certificate, an untrusted certificate and an unavailable endpoint. Verify release settings exclude debug CA trust and that failures do not silently fall back to cleartext.
evidence: Save build variant, trust configuration, endpoint and error behavior. Missing proxy traffic alone does not prove pinning is implemented.
remediation: Keep platform certificate validation intact, isolate debug overrides and plan certificate changes. Verify normal service access and rejected invalid endpoints after remediation.
question: What evidence would distinguish a confirmed issue from a tool observation in this lesson?
answer: Save build variant, trust configuration, endpoint and error behavior. Missing proxy traffic alone does not prove pinning is implemented.

title: Native libraries, JNI and memory safety
concept: JNI connects managed Android code to native libraries. Native parsers and buffers can introduce memory-safety defects that managed-language checks do not prevent.
deeper: Architecture and ABI affect analysis. Decompiled native code is approximate; symbols may be stripped. A crash is an observation, not automatic proof of exploitable code execution.
practice: Use APK Analyzer to inventory lib directories, Ghidra for a benign owned library and Android Studio LLDB for a debug native build.
workflow: Trace one JNI boundary and its length/type checks. Feed bounded malformed fixture inputs into an owned parser test harness with an available sanitizer-enabled build.
evidence: Preserve the smallest reproducer, stack trace, architecture and build flags. Separate assertion failures from out-of-bounds accesses and avoid publishing sensitive memory.
remediation: Validate sizes and lifetimes, use safer interfaces and update vulnerable dependencies. Add the reduced input to regression tests and retest supported ABIs.
question: What evidence would distinguish a confirmed issue from a tool observation in this lesson?
answer: Preserve the smallest reproducer, stack trace, architecture and build flags. Separate assertion failures from out-of-bounds accesses and avoid publishing sensitive memory.

title: Runtime analysis with controlled instrumentation
concept: Runtime observation connects static hypotheses to executed behavior. Breakpoints, method tracing and approved Frida instrumentation reveal values at a chosen boundary.
deeper: Instrumentation can alter timing and integrity checks. A hook that forces a result proves only modified behavior unless the original trust failure is separately demonstrated.
practice: Select a harmless validation method in your debug app; record its normal input and result with Android Studio before adding any instrumentation.
workflow: Compare valid and invalid synthetic input, then observe the same method with an approved tracing setup. Keep observations limited to your training process and avoid collecting real credentials.
evidence: Record the app build, process, method signature, test input and whether execution was modified. Explain coverage gaps and tool-induced differences.
remediation: Fix the underlying trust decision rather than relying only on instrumentation detection. Add source-level regression tests that run without instrumentation.
question: What evidence would distinguish a confirmed issue from a tool observation in this lesson?
answer: Record the app build, process, method signature, test input and whether execution was modified. Explain coverage gaps and tool-induced differences.

title: Integrity signals and reverse-engineering resilience
concept: Obfuscation and integrity signals can raise the cost of tampering, but client-side checks cannot be the sole authority for server-side privileges.
deeper: Root, emulator and debugger indicators have false positives and depend on implementation. Device attestation requires server-side verification and contextual policy; a client claim is not enough.
practice: Review where integrity results enter your owned app and staging backend. Model missing, stale and invalid results with test doubles.
workflow: Document which actions should be rejected, challenged or allowed. Test offline and transient-failure behavior without weakening production validation.
evidence: Show where a decision is enforced and how freshness is established. An obfuscated name or root-warning screen does not establish end-to-end protection.
remediation: Validate integrity evidence server-side, bind it to the intended request where supported and use layered controls. Retest legitimate users and failure scenarios.
question: What evidence would distinguish a confirmed issue from a tool observation in this lesson?
answer: Show where a decision is enforced and how freshness is established. An obfuscated name or root-warning screen does not establish end-to-end protection.

title: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC and USB exposure
concept: Phones expose interfaces beyond the app sandbox. Wi-Fi trust, Bluetooth pairing, NFC message handling and USB debugging each create distinct boundaries.
deeper: Radio visibility is not authorization. Encryption on one link does not imply the application protocol authenticates its peer. Nearby tests need physical scope and controlled peers.
practice: On spare owned devices, inventory enabled radios, pairing state and debugging authorizations. Use Android settings and documented test app logs.
workflow: With two owned test devices, review pairing consent and reconnection. Feed harmless NFC test data to your own reader app and verify unexpected input is rejected. Disable unused debugging trust afterward.
evidence: Record peer identity, consent steps and app-level validation. A discovered device name is not proof of compromise or identity.
remediation: Minimize exposed services, require appropriate peer authentication and validate application messages. Retest normal pairing and revocation without scanning unrelated devices.
question: What evidence would distinguish a confirmed issue from a tool observation in this lesson?
answer: Record peer identity, consent steps and app-level validation. A discovered device name is not proof of compromise or identity.

title: Mobile incident triage and evidence limits
concept: Incident triage preserves context and distinguishes observations from conclusions. Installed apps, access grants and timelines help investigate suspected compromise.
deeper: Device encryption, lock state, work profiles and tool privileges limit visibility. Bootloader unlocking or resets can destroy evidence; absence of an artifact is not proof of absence.
practice: Use a spare owned device with a documented synthetic incident timeline. Record settings and app metadata without attempting lock bypass or private-account access.
workflow: Establish timestamps, acquisition method, permissions and evidence hashes. Correlate a fictional installation with an accessibility grant and observed behavior; distinguish correlation from causation.
evidence: Keep original exports, acquisition notes and redacted working copies. Document actions that changed device state and gaps in access.
remediation: For real incidents, preserve evidence before cleanup. Recovery can include removing unauthorized access, rotating affected account credentials from a trusted device and verifying updates.
question: What evidence would distinguish a confirmed issue from a tool observation in this lesson?
answer: Keep original exports, acquisition notes and redacted working copies. Document actions that changed device state and gaps in access.

title: End-to-end mobile assessment capstone
concept: An advanced assessment combines source review, controlled runtime evidence and backend validation into a reproducible finding and regression plan.
deeper: Choose an owned demo application and one high-value boundary. Evaluate impact, prerequisites, affected builds and alternate explanations before assigning severity.
practice: Use the workbook matrix to choose one IPC, one storage and one API case. Tools should answer a specific question rather than produce an unreviewed scan dump.
workflow: For each case record setup, hypothesis, negative control, observation, remediation and retest. Run the corrected build with both rejected and legitimate input, then restore lab state.
evidence: Deliver a concise report with sanitized evidence and limitations. Do not claim hardware or OS exploit coverage from application-level tests.
remediation: Turn validated cases into regression tests and an owner-assigned remediation list. Recheck release configuration, data cleanup and supported platform differences before closing the assessment.
question: What evidence would distinguish a confirmed issue from a tool observation in this lesson?
answer: Deliver a concise report with sanitized evidence and limitations. Do not claim hardware or OS exploit coverage from application-level tests.
